findings.summary: Round one's major is fixed in two of its three sites: the backwards `presign` history survives verbatim in this javadoc, 25 lines above a comment in the SAME method that states the opposite ordering with commit ids
findings.detail: Round 1 named three sites carrying 'the third had already arrived by the time it was written'. Two are corrected: FaultInjectingStore.java:174-179 now reads '`presign` reached this class at `d5b5f21` (M5.10), fifteen hours after the row was written at `b44817a`', and backlog.md:38 reads 'FIFTEEN HOURS AFTER the row landed at `b44817a`'. I VERIFIED both against git independently: `b44817a` (M5.26) is 2026-09-10 09:34:48 +1000 and `git show b44817a~1:docs/internal/product/backlog.md | grep -c '^| M5.29 '` is 0 while the same grep at `b44817a` is 1, so the row landed there; `d5b5f21` (M5.10) is 2026-09-11 00:42:06 +1000 and `grep -c presign` on FaultInjectingStore.java is 0 at `d5b5f21~1` and 2 at `d5b5f21`. The gap is 15h07m. The two corrected sentences are true. The third site is not corrected: FaultInjectingStoreTest.java:76-80 still reads 'The M5.29 row named the first two; the third had already arrived by the time it was written, which is the row's own argument for separating the two jobs rather than adding a fourth exception.' Under the only reading in which the clause is an argument -- 'it' = the row, which the following 'the row's own argument' forces -- that is false by fifteen hours, and it is the inverse of what lines 103-105 of the same method now assert ('It reached this class at `d5b5f21` (M5.10), fifteen hours AFTER the M5.29 row predicted...'). The fix is one sentence, mirroring the text already written at FaultInjectingStore.java:174-179; this does not call for a split under rule 12, it is the unfixed residue of a round-one finding.
findings.failure_scenario: A later hand audits why `presign` -- a verb the M5.29 row never names -- was pulled into the task, opens the test that covers it, and the method javadoc says presign predated the row while a comment 25 lines down in the same method says it arrived fifteen hours after, with commit ids. One of the two is wrong and nothing in the file says which; the reader either re-does the git archaeology round one already did twice, or takes the javadoc and records the inverted history a third time -- in a file that is now the canonical place the counting/refusing split is explained.

findings.summary: `released()`'s new headline -- 'Releases that returned AND wrote the lease back' -- overstates what the guard measures: it credits an ISSUED conditional write, including one that lost the CAS and wrote nothing
findings.detail: The guard at GracefulReleaseMeter.java:62 is `completed && faulty.calls("putIfMatch") > writesBefore`, and `calls("putIfMatch")` is moved by `record("putIfMatch")` at the top of the verb (FaultInjectingStore.java:596), before any fault, any refusal and any delegate call. `LeaseManager.releaseLocked` (LeaseManager.java:452) DISCARDS the returned `Optional`: `store.putIfMatch(key, Body.ofBytes(expired.encode()), mine.version()); belief = null;`. `release()`'s own javadoc at LeaseManager.java:396-397 states the case -- 'harmless when already fenced, because the conditional write simply loses' -- so a fenced leader's release completes normally, credits `released()`, and leaves the unexpired lease on the store. The previous sentence, 'returned AND reached the store', was accurate to its guard; the replacement is accurate in the direction M5.29 fixed (a `stat` is no longer a release) and inaccurate in a new one. `issued the conditional write that releases the lease` says exactly what is measured and costs nothing. The floor itself is unaffected -- a count of issued conditional writes still goes to 0 when the release is swapped for a `stat` or deleted -- which is why this is minor.
findings.failure_scenario: Someone building a later assertion on this meter -- 'a graceful release leaves an expired lease on the store, so a successor does not wait out the TTL', which is the property LeaseManager.java:399-401 names -- reads `released()`'s javadoc, takes it as already proven, and asserts it over the sweep. It is false for every window where the leader was fenced before it closed: the CAS loses, nothing is written, the successor waits out the TTL, and `released()` counted the window.

findings.summary: M5.49 is an honest disposition, but its stated reason for preferring a reflection test over a text gate does not hold: 'every override calls `record`' IS a predicate over one file, and a grep would have caught `presign`
findings.detail: The row is real work, not a way of not doing it: it names the rung, the mechanism, the precedent it differs from, and the hard part (valid arguments for `multipart`, `getRange` and the stream verbs, and that skipping the awkward ones re-creates the hole). I verified the premise it rests on -- all twelve overrides in FaultInjectingStore.java carry a `record(...)` today, and exactly three (`capabilities`, `presign`, `close`) skip `refuseIfPartitioned`, so the enumeration everywhere in this diff is correct, and `BinStore` declares eleven methods plus `close` with none unoverridden. What does not hold is the M0.108 distinction. The rule the row wants enforced is 'no `@Override` in this file omits its `record(...)` call', which is a text predicate over a single file -- the shape backlog.md:46 says belongs in a `check-terminology.sh`-style text gate rather than in a reflection test, and the shape that WOULD have caught `presign` at `d5b5f21` without anyone invoking anything. 'Invoke the method, watch the counter' is a stronger check than the grep, but the row asserts the grep is impossible ('which no grep can express'), and that is the sentence a future implementer will act on.
findings.failure_scenario: Whoever picks up M5.49 reads 'no grep can express' as settled, skips rung 3, and writes the reflective T0 case. It lands, and it is then the second reflection-over-a-file-predicate test in the tree while M0.108 is open to strike the first -- so the same argument has to be had again, with one more test to unpick, and the cheap text gate that would have caught `presign` still does not exist.
